extracted.intended_audience: painters, art students, engravers, art critics, and connoisseurs
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative principles for truthful, brilliant landscape painting and engraving, focusing on color, light-and-shade (chiaroscuro), drawing, and spatial truth as exemplified in Turner's work. Includes guidance and anti-patterns for painters and engravers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for warm gray/green-gray over purple-gray
rubrics_metrics.description: There is perhaps nothing more characteristic of a great colorist than his power of using greens in strange places without their being felt as such, or at least than a constant preference of green gray to purple gray.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Green-gray may be permissible even when clouds are green in themselves if opposed by warm color; purple tones can be imperfect or untruthful unless corrected by warm orange and green in the foreground. Example: Poussin's cloud hue would have been allowable had there been gold or crimson enough elsewhere to throw it into gray. Anti-pattern: pure, cold, impossible purples used by 'glare-seekers' are to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early works may be false or crude in color
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of Turner’s earlier pictures (e.g., Crossing the Brook, Fall of Carthage) are cooler, greyer, or contain crude, sunless foreground tones and hence are not true pieces of color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume early mastery of color from compositional greatness; a composition may be 'glorious' yet 'not a piece of color.' Critique examples: Crossing the Brook is an agreeable cool gray rendering but 'not color'; the reddish brown foreground of the Fall of Carthage is judged 'crude, sunless, and in every way wrong.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings should be faultless and truthful as to color
rubrics_metrics.description: Turner's drawings, from earliest to latest, present an unbroken chain of increasing difficulty overcome and are, according to their aim, equally faultless as to color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings often realize an effect actually seen and so require near-separate study; as a class they should be quieter and chaster than large Academy paintings and serve as better demonstrations of intense study of nature. If better known, they would correct connoisseur judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of color to light-and-shade (chiaroscuro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turner's system subjects color entirely to light and shade; color is an auxiliary to the impression, not the source or essence of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whatever brilliancy of hue is assumed must obey the 'inviolable law of chiaroscuro'—no richness of tint should atone for the loss of arranged light, and no brilliancy should interfere with the depth of a determined shadow. The artist 'paints in color, but thinks in light and shade.' Anti-pattern: aiming at brilliancy/fire without perceiving the deep-studied shade and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness and sharpness of shadows to express vivid light
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctness of shadows is the chief means of expressing vividness of light; shadows are commonly far more conspicuous than the thing which casts them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shadows should be kept perfectly flat, keen, and even—not necessarily very dark, but with sharp edges that conceal detail of objects they cross. A pale but perfectly flat and sharp-edged shadow is more conspicuous (and conveys sunlight) than a deep shadow shaded off at the edge. Example: the edge of a close shadow is the sharpest outline nature shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blackening shadows or losing their edges (Italian school anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The old Italian masters often blacken shadows until the picture becomes appalling and lose the edges by gradation, thereby destroying appearance of sunlight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not render shadows as faint secondary daylight darknesses or smooth gradations that obliterate their sharp edges. Anti-patterns: shadows that are shaded off into surrounding tones or made excessively black so forms become invisible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make shadows clear by evenness and sharpness, not blackness
rubrics_metrics.description: Turner achieves brilliancy by making shadows clear through excessive evenness, unity, and sharpness of edge rather than by deep blackness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shadows may be faint in tone yet decisive in form; throw shadows like transparent veils across ground and air so the whole picture palpitates with them. Examples: the pavement in Hero and Leander; vignette in Rogers's Poems. Keep the darkest shadows as faint grays imbued with light rather than dense black.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use highest lights and deepest shadows only in small points and in equal quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature uses both highest lights and deepest shadows in exceedingly small quantity—always in points, never in masses—and tends to use them in equal amount so that points of one answer points of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill the mass of the picture with middle tints and pale grays, and use isolated touches of brilliant light (foam, a sail, a whitewashed cottage) and isolated deep hollows (overhanging bank, shaded figure) to give the whole its brilliancy by contrast. Avoid giving deep shadow in large quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not connect extreme lights and darks by imperceptible gradations
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperceptible gradations connecting light with shade destroy the sensation of sunshine; extreme lights and darks should be isolated and sharply separated from middle tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature covers landscape with middle tint, then touches extreme lights and extreme darks isolated and sharp so the eye goes to them directly. Anti-pattern: advice that recommends connecting light and shade by gentle gradation (this yields daylight rather than sunshine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and faithfulness of natural chiaroscuro over theatrical tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: The faithful rendering of natural light-and-shade (simple chiaroscuro in open cloudless daylight) is the true road to excellence; artificial tricks, exaggerated patterns of light and shade, and contrapuntal 'fractional' schemes are injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid painting figures 'all black' and the next 'all white', or spoiling harmony with contrived segments of sunshine and shade. Strive for the simplicity, purity, and inexhaustible variety of nature’s chiaroscuro: harmonious light expanse, decisive shadows, and delicate aerial opposition of local color. This is difficult but noble and necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shadows explain form and surface detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms and surface textures (e.g., the roughness of bark) are revealed by the agency of shadows; shadows are the chief means by which details are understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render the shadows that cut across surfaces with the sharpness and flatness necessary to reveal intervening ridges and textures; much of what we perceive as surface detail depends on these shadow relationships rather than on direct light areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of space depends primarily on drawing (focus of the eye), not hue
rubrics_metrics.description: Space is more clearly indicated by the drawing of objects (degree to which details are distinct or confused) than by their hue; drawing is an unfailing and certain criterion of distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render nearer objects with distinct details and farther objects with measured confusion to convey genuine spatial truth; aerial tone can be misleading, but drawing (focus/clarity) reliably indicates distance. Example: upper summit of a mountain can appear nearer if air is clearer—drawing solves such paradoxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot render distinct focus at unequal distances simultaneously
rubrics_metrics.description: The eye must alter focus to see objects at different distances distinctly; it is impossible to see distinct images of objects at unequal distances at the same moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In painting, simulate the eye's selective focus: make foreground crisp and detailed, reduce definition for distant forms. Anti-pattern: attempting to paint every plane with equal clarity—this destroys truth of space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engravers should not attempt to record color by particular characters of line
rubrics_metrics.description: All attempt to record color in engraving is 'heraldry out of its place': the engraver has no power beyond expressing transparency or opacity by greater or less openness of line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using different line characters to imply different colors of equal depth (this loses the system of light and shade). Engraving should prioritize the system of light-and-shade and not invent color distinctions through line types. Example anti-pattern: an area represented as coal black in engraving though a pale warm gray in the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engravers must understand and honestly represent texture within limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Texture of surface is only partly in the power of the steel and ought not to be laboriously sought after; nature's surfaces are more distinguished by form than texture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If texture is to be given, be sure you know what the texture actually is and how to represent it; avoid crude line work that misrepresents materials (e.g., turning stone into old timber, leaves given arbitrary black lines). Prefer faithful, restrained rendering; study good engravers (Miller, Goodall, Cousens) as positive examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'finish' or 'make out' what the artist intentionally omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: A fatal cause of failure in engraving is the practice of completing or finishing elements the artist left incomplete; engraver's 'improvements' often vulgarize and destroy the artist's intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect faint, tremulous lines and intentional incompleteness in the original; avoid adding features (e.g., lightning flashes, sparkling ripples) to cover shortcomings in engraving, and consult the artist where necessary rather than inventing details. Examples: added flash of lightning in Winchelsea plate; 'offensive blank windows' made definite in Dudley engraving.
